title: Rust Indexing Debt To Rust Migration Roadmap
description: 先做一轮 Rust indexing 技术债务治理，再回到继续推进 ts-indexing 切换为 rust-indexing 主线。

1.label: Rust Indexing Debt To Rust Migration Roadmap

decisions.q: What is the next strategic direction after Rust language support and CI cleanup?
decisions.answer: Do one focused technical-debt governance round first, then return to the mainline of replacing remaining TypeScript indexing responsibilities with Rust indexing where that is product-safe and evidence-backed.
decisions.note: Technical debt governance is not generic cleanup; it should reduce migration risk and make the next TS-to-Rust slices easier to reason about.

1-1.label: Technical debt governance staging before migration resumes

decisions.q: What should the debt governance round optimize for?
decisions.answer: Reduce Rust indexing migration risk and code navigation cost, not generic cleanup.
decisions.note: A debt item belongs here only if it makes later TS-to-Rust indexing migration safer, clearer, or easier to validate.

1-1-1.label: Current Rust indexing debt inventory and ownership map

decisions.q: What should the first cut produce?
decisions.answer: Produce a Rust indexing debt inventory, ownership map, and ranked next-slice candidates without changing production code.
decisions.note: This keeps the first cut as explore work so later exploit slices are chosen from evidence instead of local patch pressure.

decisions.q: How should the debt inventory be organized?
decisions.answer: Organize it by Rust indexing ownership pipeline: discovery/config, extraction, write/finalization, resolver/reference-resolution, diagnostics/status/doctor, tests/evidence.
decisions.note: Pipeline ownership keeps each debt item tied to the TS-to-Rust migration boundary it affects.

decisions.q: Should each debt item carry a next-action class?
decisions.answer: Yes. Classify every debt item as exploit-now, explore-first, or defer-no-go.
decisions.note: This prevents the inventory from becoming an undifferentiated backlog and keeps later work aligned to migration readiness.

decisions.q: What evidence bar makes the inventory credible?
decisions.answer: Every debt item needs at least one code or document anchor. Items classified as exploit-now also need a test or verification anchor.
decisions.note: The evidence bar keeps explore work concrete while making exploit candidates executable by a later TDD slice.

decisions.q: Should the first cut rewrite exploit candidates in the roadmap?
decisions.answer: Yes. Update only the 1-6 Next exploit slice candidate backlog and necessary notes, without rewriting the whole roadmap trunk.
decisions.note: The inventory must feed execution planning, but the roadmap trunk should remain stable unless the evidence shows a major direction error.

decisions.q: Where should the first-cut inventory artifact live?
decisions.answer: Keep it inside the current roadmap: write the inventory into node notes/decisions and update the 1-6 candidate backlog; do not create a separate plan document.
decisions.note: This cut is navigation calibration, not an implementation plan. Narrow plans and issues should start only after an exploit slice is selected.

decisions.q: Should the inventory cover non-code debt such as historical docs and evidence artifacts?
decisions.answer: Yes, but only document debt that can mislead migration routing or validation criteria.
decisions.note: Pure process-file cleanup stays out of the first cut unless it affects which responsibilities are still TypeScript-owned, which are Rust-owned, or which evidence is credible.

decisions.q: How should exploit-now candidates be ranked after the inventory?
decisions.answer: Prioritize low behavior risk, high migration-unlocking value, and clear test or verification anchors.
decisions.note: This favors boundary/test/fixture cleanup before risky semantic rewrites, while still serving the TS-to-Rust migration mainline.

decisions.q: Can this debt round touch crates/zcodegraph-core/src/lib.rs?
decisions.answer: Yes, but the first exploit should be behavior-preserving module-boundary or test-helper extraction, not semantic rewriting.
decisions.note: The Rust core giant module is a real migration-readiness debt, but early slices should improve navigability and testability without changing indexing behavior.

decisions.q: Should giant Rust indexing test files be exploit-now candidates?
decisions.answer: Yes. Prioritize test helper, fixture builder, and scenario splitting without changing assertion semantics.
decisions.note: Large rust-hybrid CLI and diagnostics tests are low user-behavior risk and can reduce validation cost for later migration slices.

decisions.q: How should TypeScript fallback and degraded taxonomy debt be handled in this round?
decisions.answer: Classify it as an exploit-now candidate, scoped to taxonomy/status/doctor consistency without changing fallback behavior.
decisions.note: Reliable diagnostics are a migration guardrail, but this debt pass should not silently change default indexing behavior.

decisions.q: Is candidate producer/resolver migration debt governance or the migration mainline?
decisions.answer: Treat it as explore-first in this debt round: inventory env/config/diagnostics boundaries and residuals without routing it into the main path.
decisions.note: Candidate producer is close to resolver semantic migration, so implementation should wait until the roadmap returns to the migration mainline.

decisions.q: Should CI and release guardrail debt be exploit-now in this debt round?
decisions.answer: Default it to explore-first; only CI smoke or gates that directly protect migrated Rust indexing paths can be promoted to exploit-now.
decisions.note: This keeps CI work tied to migration readiness rather than expanding into generic release hardening.

1-1-1.notes:
First-cut inventory completed. Scope: explore-only inventory, no production behavior change.

Inventory coordinate system: discovery/config -> extraction -> write/finalization -> resolver/reference-resolution -> diagnostics/status/doctor -> tests/evidence.

Debt items:
1. discovery/config: Rust core discovery and engine selection are explicit and mostly centralized (`src/indexing/rust-indexer.ts`, `src/indexing/engine-selection.ts`), but experimental candidate producer activation still has env/config boundary debt (`src/resolution/rust-candidate-producer.ts`). action=explore-first. evidence: `ZCODEGRAPH_RUST_CANDIDATE_PRODUCER`, local routing diagnostics, `__tests__/rust-index-engine-cli.test.ts`.
2. extraction: Rust core production implementation is concentrated in a giant module (`crates/zcodegraph-core/src/lib.rs`, about 20k lines). action=exploit-now for behavior-preserving module/test-helper extraction only; semantic extraction rewrites remain later migration work. evidence: `crates/zcodegraph-core/src/lib.rs`, Rust core tests.
3. write/finalization: SQLite/finalization contracts have design docs and tests, but helper boundaries remain mixed with broader Rust indexing test surfaces. action=exploit-now when scoped to helper isolation and fixture reuse. evidence: `docs/designs/rust-indexing-core-sqlite-contract.md`, `docs/designs/rust-indexing-finalization-boundary.md`, `__tests__/rust-sqlite-batching.test.ts`, `__tests__/rust-index-engine-cli.test.ts`.
4. resolver/reference-resolution: candidate producer and Rust name matcher are close to the TS-to-Rust migration mainline. action=explore-first in this debt round; do not route more resolver semantics into the main path under a debt-cleanup label. evidence: `src/resolution/rust-candidate-producer.ts`, `src/resolution/rust-name-matcher.ts`, consolidated module-resolution evidence docs.
5. diagnostics/status/doctor: fallback/degraded taxonomy is migration-critical and user-visible. action=exploit-now only for taxonomy/status/doctor consistency, with no fallback behavior change. evidence: `src/indexing/rust-hybrid-contract.ts`, `src/diagnostics/index.ts`, `src/bin/zcodegraph.ts`, `__tests__/rust-hybrid-doctor.test.ts`, `__tests__/rust-package-smoke.test.ts`.
6. tests/evidence: Rust indexing test surface has very large files, especially `__tests__/rust-index-engine-cli.test.ts` (~5k lines), making later slices costly to navigate. action=exploit-now for fixture builders, scenario split, and helper extraction without assertion-semantic changes.
7. document/evidence lifecycle: multiple consolidated Rust indexing/rust-hybrid/module-resolution docs remain useful, but stale language ownership claims or validation wording can mislead migration routing. action=explore-first, only when docs affect migration ownership or evidence credibility. evidence: `docs/benchmarks/2026-06-24-rust-hybrid-consolidated-benchmarks.md`, `docs/benchmarks/2026-06-24-rust-native-typescript-module-resolution-consolidated-evidence.md`, `docs/plans/2026-06-24-rust-indexing-ts-replacement-readiness-consolidated-plan.md`.
8. CI/release guardrails: recent Windows Rust core CI work shows this matters, but generic CI cleanup is outside this first debt pass. action=explore-first by default; promote only smoke/gates directly protecting migrated Rust indexing paths. evidence: `__tests__/ci-rust-packaged-path.test.ts`, `__tests__/release-workflow-rust-core.test.ts`, release workflow tests.

Ranked exploit-now candidates: (1) split giant Rust indexing CLI/test fixture helpers; (2) extract behavior-preserving Rust core module/test helpers from `lib.rs`; (3) isolate SQLite/finalization helper boundaries; (4) consolidate fallback taxonomy/status/doctor consistency; (5) add/adjust only Rust-migration-path CI smoke if a concrete guardrail gap is found.

Defer/no-go for this round: performance optimization as primary goal, resolver semantic routing into main path, full TypeScript indexer removal, package/node_modules expansion, and broad process-doc cleanup.

1-6.label: Next exploit slice candidate backlog

decisions.q: What makes a candidate ready for exploit?
decisions.answer: It must be bounded, testable, behavior-preserving by default, and directly connected to Rust indexing migration readiness.
decisions.note: Performance wins or new feature breadth are not enough for this backlog.

decisions.q: How should next exploit candidates be ordered after the first inventory cut?
decisions.answer: Prefer: (1) split giant Rust indexing CLI/test fixture helpers; (2) behavior-preserving Rust core module/test-helper extraction from lib.rs; (3) SQLite/finalization helper isolation; (4) fallback taxonomy/status/doctor consistency; (5) targeted Rust-migration-path CI smoke only if a concrete guardrail gap is found.
decisions.note: Ranking is recorded as execution guidance without rewriting the roadmap trunk or changing existing candidate labels.
